items.title: A Game for Two
items.passage: Tom had brought a new card game to school. At lunch, he put the cards on a table and waited. Mia stopped to look, but she did not sit down. Tom began explaining every rule, speaking faster each time she looked towards the door. Then Mia pointed at the clock and said she had only five minutes before music. Tom looked at the large pile of cards in front of him. He put most of them back in the box and left six on the table. They played one short round before Mia had to go. At the door, she asked him to bring the whole game tomorrow. Tom packed the cards with a smile. This time, he put two chairs beside the table before leaving.

questions.stem: How many cards did Tom leave on the table?
questions.evidence: He put most of them back in the box and left six on the table.

questions.stem: What did Tom learn about Mia's first reaction?

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: Choosing a different game after losing a round.
Teaching a class to play a game without cards.
Changing a plan so a friend can join in.
questions.evidence: They played one short round before Mia had to go.

items.title: The Sock Window
items.passage: Lily and Ben were putting clean socks into pairs. One blue sock was missing, although they had checked the washing basket twice. Ben looked under the table and behind the door. Lily picked up a white shirt from the basket and noticed something blue through the thin cloth. She put her hand inside a sleeve and pulled out the missing sock. Ben laughed and held up another shirt like a window. There was nothing inside that one, but he checked the rest before putting them down. Soon, every sock had a partner. Lily placed the last blue pair on top of the pile. Ben put the empty basket on his head for a moment. Lily told him to check it first, in case there was another sock hiding inside.

items.title: The Picture You Can Hear
items.passage: Sam and Zoe were drawing the same playground after school. Sam filled his page with swings, trees, and children. Zoe drew just a tree with little curved marks around it. Sam asked why her picture had so few things. Zoe pointed towards the branches, where leaves were moving in the wind. She said the marks showed the soft sound she could hear. Sam looked at his busy page again. He had drawn a ball beside two children, but their game seemed strangely quiet. He added marks around the bouncing ball and wrote a word for its sound. Zoe smiled and added a bird to her tree. When they showed their pictures to the teacher, Sam asked her to listen. She looked surprised, so he pointed to the marks and explained.

questions.stem: What did Zoe draw first?
options: A ball with marks around it.
A tree with marks around it.
A bird with marks around it.
questions.evidence: Zoe drew just a tree with little curved marks around it.

questions.stem: What gave Sam his new idea for the ball?
options: Zoe showed that a larger ball was easier to see.
Zoe showed that the page needed another tree.
Zoe showed that marks could suggest a sound.
questions.evidence: She said the marks showed the soft sound she could hear.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: Finding a way to show sounds in pictures.
Choosing the quietest place to draw outside.
Learning to draw a playground from a photograph.
questions.evidence: He added marks around the bouncing ball and wrote a word for its sound.

items.title: The Practice Reader
items.passage: Raj was going to read his short story to the class on Friday. At home, he read it to Ella, but he kept stopping to ask if she liked it. Ella answered every question, and they never reached the last page. The next evening, she put a toy rabbit on a chair. She sat beside it and asked Raj to read to the rabbit first. Raj nearly stopped after the first page, then looked at its quiet face and went on. He reached the ending before asking Ella anything. She told him which part had made her laugh. On Friday, Raj pictured the rabbit while he stood in front of the class. He read the whole story, then looked up. Several children were smiling at the same funny ending.

Choosing a toy to take to a classroom show.

items.title: The Visitor at the Window
items.passage: Nina was drawing at a low window while Omar read beside her. Their cat jumped onto the wide seat below the glass and watched Nina move her pencil. Whenever she lifted it, the cat reached towards its bright red end. Nina put the pencil down, but the cat stayed, looking at her hand. Omar brought its toy mouse and moved it across the floor. The cat jumped down to follow, leaving Nina room to draw. She finished a picture of the cat with one foot in the air. Then she put the pencil in a drawer and showed Omar her page. He held it near the cat, but the cat walked past without looking. Omar laughed that the cat had liked the moving pencil much more than its own picture.

questions.stem: What did Omar bring for the cat?

questions.stem: What most likely caught the cat's attention at the window?

questions.evidence: Whenever she lifted it, the cat reached towards its bright red end.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: Teaching a cat to sit still while someone draws its picture.
Helping a child finish drawing by giving her cat something else to follow.
Finding a lost toy by watching where a cat looks.
questions.evidence: The cat jumped down to follow, leaving Nina room to draw.

items.title: Two Views of One Tree
items.passage: Amir and Sara stood on opposite sides of a tree in the school playground. Their teacher asked them to draw what they could see without moving. Amir drew a short branch near the ground. Sara drew a round hole higher up. When they compared their drawings, each thought the other had added something that was not there. They asked the teacher which picture was right. Instead of choosing, she asked them to exchange places and look again. Amir could now see the hole, while Sara found the low branch partly hidden by leaves. They turned their papers over and made a second drawing. Back in class, they put all four pictures together. Amir said their tree seemed to have grown two new parts, although it had not changed.

questions.stem: What did Sara draw in her first picture?
options: A round hole in the tree.
A bird sitting on a branch.
A flower growing near the tree.
questions.evidence: Sara drew a round hole higher up.

questions.stem: Why did the teacher ask them to exchange places?
options: To help them see what the other child could see.
To give them more space for their drawing paper.
To keep the sunlight out of both children's eyes.
questions.evidence: Amir could now see the hole, while Sara found the low branch partly hidden by leaves.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: Deciding which child can draw a tree more accurately.
Finding that different views can both be right.
Discovering how quickly a tree grows new branches.
questions.evidence: Back in class, they put all four pictures together.

items.title: The Round That Did Not Count
items.passage: Max and Priya made a game in which players rolled a ball towards three boxes. The nearest box was worth one point, and the farthest was worth three. Priya scored eight points before Max noticed that one box had moved. Each time the ball touched it, the light box slid a little farther across the floor. Max had been playing after Priya, so his throws had started with the box farther away. They put a book inside each box to stop it moving. Priya suggested starting again with no points. Max agreed, and they tested one throw each before the new round. This time, all three boxes stayed in place. Priya still scored eight points. Max smiled and said he could believe those eight much more easily.

questions.stem: What did they put inside the boxes?
questions.evidence: They put a book inside each box to stop it moving.

questions.stem: Why did they start again with no points?
options: They had forgotten which box was worth three.
The moving box had made the turns unequal.
The ball had broken before Max could play.
questions.evidence: Max had been playing after Priya, so his throws had started with the box farther away.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: Finding and fixing a problem that made a game unfair.
Learning to throw a ball farther to get more points.
Making a game shorter by taking one box out.
questions.evidence: This time, all three boxes stayed in place.

items.title: The Space in the Song
items.reviewNote: İkinci doğru şık riski: keyboard doğru, 'piano' çocuk için de doğru sayılabilir. Piano yerine drum/recorder.
items.passage: Jack and Aisha had written a song for a little classroom show. Jack sang the words while Aisha played four notes on a keyboard. At the end of each line, Jack took a breath, but Aisha started the next part immediately. He kept arriving a word behind the music. They tried singing faster, then playing more slowly, but neither change felt right. Aisha asked Jack to sing without the keyboard while she listened. This time, she noticed the little spaces between his lines. She marked those places on her paper and waited there when they tried together again. Jack finished each breath before the next notes began. At the show, they reached the last word together. Afterwards, Jack said that Aisha had played the quiet parts very well too.

questions.evidence: Jack sang the words while Aisha played four notes on a keyboard.

questions.stem: What did Jack mean by the quiet parts?
options: The notes Aisha played too softly to hear.
The pauses when Aisha waited for his breath.
The words Jack forgot during the show.
questions.evidence: She marked those places on her paper and waited there when they tried together again.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: Listening to each other to make a song work.
Finding a louder instrument for a classroom show.
Writing easier words so a song can be sung quickly.
questions.evidence: Jack finished each breath before the next notes began.

items.title: The Afternoon Circle
items.passage: Meera noticed a round patch of light on the classroom wall after lunch. In the morning, that part of the wall had been plain. Dan thought someone had painted a circle while the class was outside. Meera moved her hand across it, and the circle appeared on her hand instead. They looked towards the window, where a small round mirror stood on a table. Their teacher carefully turned the mirror, and the bright circle moved across the wall. She turned it towards the table, and the circle moved there too. Dan brought his drawing over and held it beside the light, keeping it out of his eyes. His paper sun now had a bright circle beside it. Before going home, he put the drawing on the wall where the light had first appeared.

questions.stem: What stood on the table near the window?
questions.evidence: They looked towards the window, where a small round mirror stood on a table.

questions.stem: What showed that the circle was not painted on the wall?
options: It was round rather than square.
It appeared after the class had lunch.
questions.evidence: Meera moved her hand across it, and the circle appeared on her hand instead.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: Working out what made a changing patch of light.
Finding the best place to hang a classroom painting.
Learning to draw a circle without a round object.
questions.evidence: Their teacher carefully turned the mirror, and the bright circle moved across the wall.

items.title: The Dragon Who Packed Too Much
items.passage: Ravi was writing a comic about a dragon going on a picnic. Yan drew a bag full of cups, plates, books, and a huge blanket. In the next picture, the dragon tried to fly, but the bag stayed on the ground. Ravi wanted the dragon to reach a hill for its picnic. Yan suggested drawing a smaller bag, but Ravi liked all the things inside the big one. They looked at the first picture again. It showed the dragon waiting beside a little cart. Yan drew the dragon putting the bag in the cart and pulling it along the path. At the hill, the dragon opened the blanket for its friends. Ravi added one last picture of the empty cart. A sleepy rabbit had chosen it for a bed.

questions.stem: What did the dragon put in the cart?
options: The friends going to the picnic.
The books borrowed from a library.
